summary: Jeremiah 39 (18 verses) continues the story of judgment. Starting with 'In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem, and besieged it.', it moves through themes of judgment, new covenant and calls readers toward tears.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows judgment lived out in jerusalem falling. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem, and besieged it.
But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left of the poor of the people, who had nothing, in the land of Judah, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.
For I will surely save you. You won’t fall by the sword, but you will escape with your life, because you have put your trust in me,” says Yahweh.’”

questions.question: What is happening in Jeremiah 39?
questions.answer: In 18 verses, this chapter jeremiah 39 (18 verses) continues the story of judgment. starting with 'in the ninth year of zedekiah king of judah, in the tenth month, nebuchadnezzar king of babylon and all his army came against jerusalem, and besieged it.', it moves through themes of judgment, new covenant and calls readers toward tears. The setting is jerusalem falling, written to judah before exile. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Jeremiah and why 39 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally jeremiah, addressed to judah before exile around ~600 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as prophetic laments — its themes of judgment, new covenant build on what came before.

questions.question: Are there any difficult words here?
questions.answer: Scan for names, places, or repeated abstract words like righteousness, covenant, or glory. The glossary below defines up to 3 that show up most. Ask: who is this person, what does this word mean in everyday terms?

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through judgment and new covenant, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 5 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them, and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. When they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to Riblah...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about judgment. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
